To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the dictator's ability to exploit the population and to maximize his own welfare depends on the distribution of natural resources across the population and the distribution of these resources among the groups in the society.
the dictator may foster civil war to hold on power.
a dictator may foster civil war in order to enhance the tax base of his country.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new and intriguing question in the literature: can civil war be used as a policy instrument to maximize the ruler's rents?
the question of why some autocrats are more successful than others in maintaining their power.
the question how autocrats can use civil war to enhance their power and how they can exploit the natural resources of their country.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the autocrat may use the ethnic division as a tool to increase his power and the tax rate, and thus the rent he collects.
the autocrat is not averse to civil war.
the ruling elite is not only interested in divide and rule but also in spark and rule, i.e. to create and maintain civil war.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the autocrat may be tempted to exacerbate existing group antagonisms to enhance his taxing power.
a dictator may use ethnic division to his benefit, even if he does not have any ethnic affiliation.
a weak autocrat can increase his rent by fostering civil strife.
The main takeaway from our work is that
autocrats may use the spark of civil strife to enhance their taxing capacity.
the dictator's choice of the tax rate is not necessarily a reflection of the society's ethnic composition.
the ruler's choice of policies is driven not by his desire to promote social cohesion or economic development, but by his need to maximize his own rents.
